## Why it appeared

**KIAA1614** had the highest methylation frequency of the three validated promoter-panel genes in the cited UC series, with reduced RNA expression [Kang et al.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5000688/).

The underlying evidence came from a small 450K discovery set (8 UC, 3 controls), followed by targeted technical validation in 79 UC samples and bulk qRT-PCR [@kang2016ucpanel]. “Highest frequency” therefore refers to this selected panel and cohort; it is not a population prevalence estimate or an independently validated clinical sensitivity.

## Function and loss

[NCBI’s curated record](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/57710) lists predicted involvement in centrosome cycle, establishment or maintenance of cell polarity, and regulation of cellular localization, with predicted activity at the apical membrane, cortex, and nucleus. Much of this annotation is computational rather than direct human intestinal evidence.

If genuine loss disrupted epithelial polarity, one could imagine altered apical–basal organization or repair. That is a **testable hypothesis**, not a result. Lower bulk-tissue RNA could also reflect fewer expressing cells rather than repression within each cell.

## Biomarker before mechanism

Near-term work should treat the locus as a candidate classifier: lock the assayed CpGs, test inflammation-matched disease controls, and validate externally. Mechanistic work can proceed in parallel, but predicted Gene Ontology annotations should not be used as evidence that KIAA1614 controls colon polarity.

<details><summary><strong>Best next experiment</strong></summary>

Localize KIAA1614 in colon cell types, perturb it in polarized organoids, and measure junction placement, centrosomes, wound closure, and rescue while confirming the promoter methylation state.
</details>
